title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 1. How are Time Spy and Steel Nomad scored, and what do they render?
t: 1. How are Time Spy and Steel Nomad scored, and what do they render? Time Spy. Two graphics tests (2560x1440) and a CPU test. The overall score is a weighted harmonic mean: (W_g + W_c) / (W_g / S_g + W_c / S_c), with the graphics weight 0.85 and the CPU weight 0.15 [1]. The graphics score is the harmonic mean of the two tests' average frame rates times a scaling constant, which brings it in line with traditional 3DMark levels; the CPU score derives from simulation time per frame [1]. A harmonic mean means a weak CPU or GPU drags the total down more than an arithmetic mean would [1]. Steel Nomad. Rendering resolution 3840 x 2160, DirectX 12 feature level 12 or Vulkan 1.1, one graphics test and no CPU test [2]. The overall score equals the graphics score, which is the average frame rate times 100 [3]. Speed Way uses the same rule: score = average FPS x 100 [4]. What Steel Nomad renders (UL's "engine" page) [5]: opaque objects with deferred rendering into a G-buffer with PBR material parameters, shading in linear HDR; order-independent transparency; decals; reflections and diffuse global illumination sampled from probes spread around the scene; GPU-simulated particles (compute shaders); grass in compute shaders with distance-based level of detail; a dynamic ray-marched volumetric cloud sky; screen-space contact shadows; screen-space reflections with a cube-map fallback; heat distortion from particles; compute-shader FFT bloom (blur, streaks, anamorphic flare, lenticular halo); a three-pass froxel volume illumination for fog; scatter-as-gather depth of field; and XeGTAO ambient occlusion (ultra quality in compute shaders in Steel Nomad, high quality in pixel shaders in Light) [5]. Steel Nomad uses asynchronous compute to overlap the first volume-illumination pass with other passes; Light does not, and also has no volume illumination [5]. It is explicitly non-ray-traced [6]. Version history: 1.0, launch version, and no later version [7].

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 2. How big is 3DMark's user base, and who holds records?
t: 2. How big is 3DMark's user base, and who holds records? UL gives few total figures. Hard numbers from UL: Time Spy had "almost 48 million" submitted results by May 2024 [6]; the Android app had "more than 100,000 downloads in its first week" (April 2013) and the iOS app 50,000 downloads in two weeks (September 2013) [8]; UL describes the 3DMark Hall of Fame as the home of world-record scores [9]. A third-party download page claims "25 years, 50M+ results" but I could not trace that to UL, so I treat it as unconfirmed [10]. I found no UL total for all results or for active users. Records: cached Hall of Fame pages show Port Royal's top entries in the high 40,000s on RTX 5090 systems (for example 47,311 on an RTX 5090 with a Core i9-14900KS at rank 85 in one snapshot), and an old Time Spy snapshot headed by multi-GPU rigs [9]. The pages carry a notice about turbulence and the snapshots are of different dates, so these are not current standings. HWBot and the Hall of Fame both hold records; I did not reconcile them. Not confirmed.

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 3. The 3DMark03 driver scandal and the smartphone delistings
t: 3. The 3DMark03 driver scandal and the smartphone delistings May 2003. An ExtremeTech investigation of Nvidia's drivers prompted a Futuremark audit [11]. On Friday 23 May 2003, Futuremark published a seven-page audit of Detonator FX 44.03 and 43.51 drivers listing eight instances where it believed Nvidia modified drivers unfairly; renaming the benchmark executable lowered scores in certain tests [11][12]. Futuremark's patch 330 stops the drivers recognising the benchmark; it measured the GeForce FX 5900 Ultra dropping about 24% with it, versus under 2% for ATI's Radeon 9800 Pro [12]. The Register (27 May 2003) reported ATI also admitted tweaks: renaming the executable cut Game Test 4 by 8% and the total by just under 2% (ATI said it was an optimization of the water and sky shaders, "mathematically and functionally identical", and promised to remove it) [11]. Weeks later Futuremark reversed course: it said Nvidia's approach was an "application specific optimization" rather than a cheat, but still said the rules were broken, and did not reinstate the original results; a joint statement called for clear industry rules for benchmarks [13]. Phones. On 7 September 2018 UL delisted the Huawei P20 Pro, Nova 3 and Honor Play (and the P20 based on AnandTech's testing). UL compared the public 3DMark app with a private build that is not available to manufacturers: public-app scores were up to 47% higher with identical tests, meaning the phones recognised the app by name. Delisted devices appear unranked, without scores [14]. Other delistings reported: OPPO's Find X and F7 (2018) and a 2013 sweep of HTC and Samsung Android devices [15]; and in April 2020 MediaTek-based phones from Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, Sony and Realme [16].

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 4. The Time Spy asynchronous compute controversy
t: 4. The Time Spy asynchronous compute controversy In July 2016 a forum post on Overclock.net argued Time Spy's async compute use fit Nvidia's architecture better than AMD's: in DOOM and Ashes of the Singularity the Fury X beat a GTX 1070, but not in Time Spy [17]. PC Perspective explained the issue and noted the causes were unknown (driver maturity, optimization differences) [17]. Futuremark replied on 19 July 2016 with a detailed post. Its main points: Time Spy was developed with input from AMD, Intel, Microsoft, NVIDIA and others in the Benchmark Development Program, in development for nearly two years; vendors spent weeks in the office, downloaded daily source drops hundreds of times, and exchanged "around one thousand emails" on it; the engine uses two queues, DIRECT and COMPUTE, regardless of the hardware; "the implementation is the same regardless of the underlying hardware" with no vendor-specific optimizations; and whether COMPUTE-queue work runs in parallel or serial "is ultimately the decision of the underlying driver" because DirectX 12 only lets an application permit parallel execution [18]. The post shows GPUView traces for the GTX 970, Fury and GTX 1080 with async compute on and off, and the compute work items: particle simulation, light culling and tiling, environment reflections, HBAO and unshadowed surface illumination [18]. Futuremark's stated principle is that 3DMark predicts games in general, not absolute theoretical maximums [18]. Forum claims that Nvidia's driver disables async on pre-Pascal cards, or that Time Spy's version is "preemption based", are unconfirmed forum claims [19].

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 5. Which feature tests exist, and when did they arrive?
t: 5. Which feature tests exist, and when did they arrive? From UL's About-page timeline and release notes [8][20]: Date Feature test March 2015 API Overhead, "the world's first DirectX 12 API performance test" (Vulkan added March 2017; Android Vulkan August 2017) June 2016 Stress tests added (loop runs to check stability) February 2019 NVIDIA DLSS feature test (DLSS 2 and three quality modes added September 2020; DLSS 3 and Frame Generation October 2022) June 2019 PCI Express bandwidth feature test August 2019 VRS feature test (Tier 2 option added December 2019) October 2020 DirectX Raytracing feature test February 2021 Mesh Shader feature test June 2021 CPU Profile (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 or max threads) August 2021 Sampler Feedback feature test November 2021 Storage Benchmark (a paid add-on) October 2022 Intel XeSS feature test March 2023 AMD FSR feature test (release notes: 30 March 2023, "FSR 2") October 2024 Opacity Micromap feature test (Android) November 2024 DirectStorage feature test The Mesh Shader test, per UL, uses a hall of carved pillars: one pass culls with the traditional approach, a second with mesh shaders, to show how game engines can boost frame rates [21]. UL's Sampler Feedback test (24 August 2021 per its news post; the timeline says August 2021) made 3DMark the first public app with all four DirectX 12 Ultimate features, according to UL's coverage [20][22].

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 6. The mobile tests
t: 6. The mobile tests UL's timeline gives: 3DMark for Android in April 2013 (100,000+ downloads in the first week), iOS in September 2013 (50,000 in two weeks), Windows RT in October 2013 [8]. Ice Storm and Ice Storm Extreme were released in 2013 and support ended on 14 January 2020 (Ice Storm used OpenGL ES 2.0 on mobile) [23]. Sling Shot (OpenGL ES 3.1 and 3.0) arrived on Android in July 2015 and iOS in October 2015, with Sling Shot Extreme using Apple's Metal in March 2016 [8]. Wild Life arrived in October 2020 as a cross-platform benchmark for Apple, Android and Windows (Vulkan on Windows and Android; 2560 x 1440) [8][24]. Wild Life Extreme followed in May 2021 at 3840 x 2160, for Windows notebooks, Arm PCs and Apple M1 Macs [8][24]. Solar Bay launched in August 2023 as a ray-tracing benchmark: Vulkan 1.1, a benchmark whose ray-traced workload increases linearly by 100% over three stages with four scores, plus a stress test that loops for 20 minutes; the app was previously "3DMark Wild Life Benchmark" [25]. Steel Nomad Light (May 2024) is the 1440p test for lighter devices [24]. Solar Bay Extreme followed in August 2025 [8].

t: 7. What has 3DMark cost? title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 8. Other Futuremark benchmarks, and the Vantage PhysX dispute
t: 8. Other Futuremark benchmarks, and the Vantage PhysX dispute From UL's timeline [8]: Final Reality (May 1997, Remedy, before the company existed) [30]; PCMark2002 (March 2002); PCMark04 (November 2003); PCMark05 (June 2005); PCMark Vantage (October 2007); Peacekeeper (March 2009, free browser test; universal-browser version November 2011); PCMark 7 (May 2011); Powermark (December 2011); PCMark 8 (June 2013 Professional); PCMark for Android (October 2014); VRMark (November 2016; Cyan Room November 2017); PCMark 10 (June 2017); Testdriver (July 2017); Servermark (November 2017 onward); Procyon (September 2020). Peacekeeper support ended on 29 July 2015 [31]. The UL timeline states 3DMark06 (January 2006) was "our most popular 3DMark yet" and Fire Strike Ultra (October 2014) the "world's first 4K Ultra HD benchmark" and Time Spy Extreme (October 2017) the "world's first 4K DirectX 12 benchmark test" [8]. Vantage PhysX. Nvidia's ForceWare 177.39 drivers let 3DMark Vantage's CPU physics test run on the GPU, via PhysX, inflating the CPU score; reports quote CPU Test 2 at about 15 FPS without and 128 FPS with GPU PhysX [32]. Nvidia said this was a physics test, not a graphics test; AMD and others objected. Futuremark's CEO said GPU PhysX would not be allowed because the CPU test measures CPU physics, and Futuremark updated its Hall of Fame to exclude GPU PhysX results [32]. I did not retrieve Futuremark's own statement or exact dates, and some reports conflict on stages of the policy. Partly confirmed.

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 9. How does the Benchmark Development Program work?
t: 9. How does the Benchmark Development Program work? UL describes it as industry cooperation: each 3DMark "was developed with input from" AMD, Intel, NVIDIA and other members of the "UL Benchmark Development Program" [2][24]. The fullest account is Futuremark's own July 2016 post: members receive regular builds throughout development and conduct their own testing at each stage; they have source-code access and can suggest changes; all work is in a single source tree, so anything suggested by a vendor can be seen; vendors reviewed Time Spy for weeks in the office; and when members disagree, Futuremark listens to all sides, consults game developers, and asks "Is this the approach a game developer would take?" [18]. Futuremark says vendors are invariably against vendor-specific paths, because they would alter the work done and break comparability [18]. A forum claim that Futuremark cannot publish unless all vendors approve is unconfirmed [19]. UL's 2026 Seasonic sponsorship shows another input: UL says the sponsor's logo is displayed inside the benchmark [33]; it does not say what sponsors pay or whether they influence the test. UL's BDP page was not retrievable; a full member list is not confirmed.

title: 3DMark: supplementary answers
h: 10. How were Port Royal and Speed Way received, and how do they relate to games?
t: 10. How were Port Royal and Speed Way received, and how do they relate to games? Port Royal launched on 8 January 2019 at 2560 x 1440, requiring DirectX Raytracing, as "the world's first dedicated real-time ray tracing benchmark for gamers" [34]. Early press tests: one put the RTX 2080 at 5,986 (28 FPS) and the RTX 2080 Ti at 7,925 (37 FPS); another saw an ASUS ROG Strix RTX 2080 OC at 6,106 [35]. Reviewers noted that the GTX 1080 fell far behind in this test, and that Port Royal does not run at maximum quality for ray tracing (one outlet measured an RTX 2080 Ti dropping from 37.8 to 23.0 FPS at lower ray-tracing quality) [35]. NVIDIA added DLSS to the benchmark in February 2019, claiming up to 50% more performance [35]. Speed Way launched on 12 October 2022 for DirectX 12 Ultimate (feature level 12_2), at 2560 x 1440 [4][36]. Its engine removes all precomputed lighting (no lightmaps or probes), is fully dynamic, uses mesh shaders for continuous level-of-detail selection and culling, a deferred direct-lighting path, and DirectX Raytracing 1.1 for global illumination and reflections [4][36]. It was sponsored by Lenovo Legion [36]. UL's pricing moved to $34.99 with it [26]. Typical RTX 4090 results in forums run around 10,000 to 12,000 [37]; one overclocker record was later deemed invalid by 3DMark due to a VRAM artifacting bug (a forum report) [37]. Relationship to games. UL's stated aim is to predict game performance generally, not the theoretical maximum of the hardware, through a neutral, common code path [18]. UL also publishes a support article on estimating game performance from scores; I could not retrieve it, so I cannot quote its guidance. Tom's Hardware uses a FurMark run as a power worst-case rather than 3DMark as a game proxy [38]. Independent studies of how well 3DMark scores predict frame rates in particular games: not found.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 1. Who is 'Steel Nomad'? Is there a named hero with a backstory?
t: 1. Who is 'Steel Nomad'? Is there a named hero with a backstory? Official designation: Steel Nomad is the title of UL Solutions' 2024 3DMark benchmark and its setting, described as a frontier to explore [N1][N2]. The image most viewers associate with it is a lone masked figure in hard-wearing, red-brown clothing/armour and a broad, Asian-conical-hat-shaped metal helmet. Several launch reviewers describe the glowing blue eyes and its robotic or cyborg appearance [N3][N4]. It is reasonable to refer to this figure as 'the Nomad' as shorthand , but that is not a confirmed legal name. What is not established: No publisher source found here gives the protagonist a personal name, age, maker, faction, species, gender, home planet, origin quest or lines of dialogue. There is no verified character biography, game franchise or tie-in novel. 'A wandering robot seeking X' is tempting but not official canon . Interpretation: The anonymous wanderer creates an instantly readable science-fiction western archetype—an outsider entering an unfamiliar settlement. The design tells a visual story without needing dialogue, useful for a short, repeatable benchmark.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 2. Where does the Nomad come from, and what journey do we see?
t: 2. Where does the Nomad come from, and what journey do we see? Observed scene, not official character script: Reviews of the benchmark describe a masked rider arriving on a futuristic hovering motorcycle-like vehicle , entering a settlement, moving past a bar/other inhabitants and looking towards an overlook with a caravan or distant structures [N3][N5]. Launch screenshots show a dense industrial town, sunlit rock formations and a panoramic view of distant islands, bridges and structures [N3][N4]. In another frame the traveller examines an illuminated circular device [N3]. We should distinguish a visually shown arrival from a documented route map. UL does not publish an in-world starting city, the traveller's home, a journey distance, a quest objective or a guaranteed scene-by-scene plot synopsis [N1][N2]. The third-party sequence above describes the reviewer's observations, not an official script. Interpretation: Vehicle arrival → frontier settlement → curious artefact/viewpoint is a classic 'traveller finds a strange civilisation' miniature narrative. Its shape communicates curiosity, not a confirmed mission.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 3. Is this a post-apocalyptic Earth, distant alien planet or future frontier?
t: 3. Is this a post-apocalyptic Earth, distant alien planet or future frontier? Canon: UL calls the setting a frontier and describes the heavy benchmark as taking place in a sun-scorched environment [N1][N6]. Its landscapes include a desert basin with built structures; Steel Nomad Light's setting is the same basin at night and flooded by a vast lake , as publisher and storefront descriptions explicitly state [N6][N7]. Observed: Rock formations, makeshift buildings, automated-looking infrastructure, hovering transport, robots or masks, distant metallic structures and spectacular skies make it look like post-apocalyptic or far-future science fiction [N3][N4][N5]. Unverified: No reliable UL source establishes a planet, date, war, collapse, extraterrestrial arrival, resource scarcity, or shared timeline with Time Spy, Port Royal or earlier 3DMark scenes. The correct wording is science-fiction frontier aesthetic , not 'canonically post-apocalyptic Earth'.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 4. Is the wanderer a robot, cyborg or human in armour?
t: 4. Is the wanderer a robot, cyborg or human in armour? Observed: Close-up coverage shows glowing blue eyes behind a metal face covering, a textured hood/helmet, layered protective clothing and mechanical-looking devices at the chest [N3][N4]. The movement and environment suggest robots/androids to some reviewers [N5]. The word 'Steel' and cybernetic/industrial styling strengthen that reading. But there is no verified biological reveal. The helmet could conceal a person; blue lights could be optics in a robotic head or a mask. We cannot reliably choose among robot, cyborg, humanoid alien or armoured human from external imagery alone. No maker-supplied character sheet, biography, voice line or anatomical evidence found here settles it. The intriguing truth is that the character is visually legible as a wanderer yet biologically ambiguous —possibly deliberately, though that intent itself is unconfirmed.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 5. Who lives here? Are the caravans, machines and town an organised society?
t: 5. Who lives here? Are the caravans, machines and town an organised society? Observed: The benchmark's setting shows a small settlement , with signs of commerce, shelters, transport machines, other humanoid/mechanical figures and a passing caravan described in contemporary reviews [N5]. Some accounts mention a bar and the traveller parking or charging the transport [N5]. These details are observations, not confirmed job assignments or factions . Interpretation: The bar, transit lanes, public equipment and other travellers suggest a place where people/robots live and exchange goods rather than an empty stage. The battered surfaces imply age and use. The scene has enough environmental cues for players to imagine a town's history. Unverified: The settlement's official name, governance, economy, species, language, trading partners, whether the caravan carries goods or refugees, and whether the Nomad knows its residents. Treating every robotic prop as an actual named NPC would overstate the evidence.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 6. What is the glowing sphere or blue ring—and what is the Nomad trying to do?
t: 6. What is the glowing sphere or blue ring—and what is the Nomad trying to do? Observed: 4Gamer's May 2024 visual coverage includes a frame showing the masked figure beside a circular apparatus projecting an intense blue light , with mechanical or display components around it [N3]. Other screenshots show glowing distant objects in the dramatic landscape [N4]. These are genuine scene elements, not an invented item. Unknown: Public UL launch material does not supply a name, mechanism, function or mission text for this apparatus [N1][N2]. It might be a console, communications terminal, transport device, power source, holographic display or simply a scene prop. None of those hypotheses can be asserted as the true explanation . Interpretation: The scene uses recognisable science-fiction machinery to create a moment of investigation, just as Superposition uses the professor's apparatus. The difference is that Steel Nomad does not have a similarly explicit official disappearance mystery or objective.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 7. Why does Steel Nomad Light show the desert flooded at night? Is it a sequel?
t: 7. Why does Steel Nomad Light show the desert flooded at night? Is it a sequel? Canon: UL and its product listings say Steel Nomad Light takes place at night , with the desert basin flooded by a vast lake , and uses a lighter 1440p workload with fewer or reduced demanding techniques. The standard Steel Nomad is the sunlit 4K benchmark [N6][N7]. This contrast creates two distinct images of one visual world. What we can conclude: The setting is transformed between two versions, and the change in light, water and atmospheric effects supports different artistic and performance requirements. What we cannot conclude: There is no verified canonical time jump, flood catastrophe, climate story, death or resurrection explaining why the lake appeared. Light is a workload variant, not an announced narrative sequel. Interpretation: A flooded moonlit frontier makes an evocative alternative state—quiet, eerie and flooded compared with daylight's heat and bustle. It opens up lore questions without proving the answer.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 8. Which Easter eggs link Steel Nomad to older 3DMark worlds?
t: 8. Which Easter eggs link Steel Nomad to older 3DMark worlds? Canon: UL made Steel Nomad partly as a 25th-anniversary celebration , previewing the world in November 2023 and announcing that the environment would contain callbacks to many earlier benchmarks [N2]. Its May 2024 launch specifically promised secret locations and Easter eggs throughout Explorer Mode [N1]. Independent identification: A PC Gamer reviewer spotted a flying robot from Port Royal and butterflies from 3DMark 2001 [N8]. Those are named contemporary reviewer observations , not an official exhaustive catalogue. The 3DMark Steel Explorer achievement specifically refers to finding all secret areas and hidden treasures [N9]. Do not overread: A returning model or butterfly is evidence of a deliberate tribute, not evidence that Steel Nomad, Port Royal and 3DMark 2001 share a canonical timeline or that the same person appears across tests. A full verified Easter-egg catalogue would require an Explorer Mode survey with screenshots and precise locations.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 9. Why is there sound again, and what extra story does Explorer Mode unlock?
t: 9. Why is there sound again, and what extra story does Explorer Mode unlock? Canon: UL explicitly announced that it had brought back sound due to popular demand [N1]. Explorer Mode lets a user roam the scene, change rendering settings and camera composition, and find otherwise missed secret locations and references [N1][N7]. The official launch recommends playing with sound . Demo users can run the test, but Explorer Mode is part of the purchased 3DMark experience [N1]. Storytelling benefit (interpretation): Ambient sounds and a freely moving viewpoint make the settlement feel like a place rather than merely a graphics workload. You can see details a scripted camera passes over and form your own account of the world's inhabitants. It is an example of environmental storytelling alongside benchmark utility. Boundary: UL does not present Explorer Mode as a full role-playing game with NPC conversations, branching quests or a confirmed final story revelation. 'Discover secret locations' is supported; 'complete the Nomad's quest' is not.

title: The masked wanderer: scene and lore
h: 10. Is there an official novel-like story, design rationale or confirmed ending?
t: 10. Is there an official novel-like story, design rationale or confirmed ending? Based on publisher material reviewed: no fully published character plot was established. UL advertises the visual frontier , the benchmarks' 25th-anniversary callbacks, gameplay-like rendering techniques and the option to explore [N1][N2][N6]. The promotional copy intentionally invokes western language—'strides into town', 'this town is big enough' and 'explore the frontier'—but does not explain the traveller's name, destination or ultimate fate [N1]. Design context: Steel Nomad replaced Time Spy as UL's flagship heavy, non-ray-traced test because modern GPUs needed a more demanding, cross-platform scene [N1]. The art uses volumetric clouds, grass generated by compute shaders, screen-space reflections, fog lighting, elaborate materials and depth-of-field [N10]. A dry, rugged frontier gives those features rocks, grass, water, buildings, people and changing skies to render. That is a technical rationale for the setting's suitability , not proof of the creator's personal artistic inspiration. Open creator questions: Is the Nomad human? Who built the transport? What is the blue device? Are the ancient structures connected to other 3DMark worlds? Is the Light lake a future, parallel state or simply an alternate scene treatment? These remain unanswered by trustworthy available official evidence . Recording that gap is more accurate than fan-fiction presented as fact.

title: My GTX 1070 batch: deep research
h: The main discoveries
t: The main discoveries The sheet contains 100 numbered slots , 38 marked GPU-Z recognised (cards 1–38), 37 FurMark scores , 35 Superposition scores , 35 Steel Nomad scores , and 35 cards with all three . The 100 rows are inventory slots , not a confirmed stocktake of 100 cards. A prior conversation estimated 92 physical cards; that quantity still requires serial/label reconciliation. Every one of the 37 FurMark result URLs was opened; 36 link to a GTX 1070 with the correct sheet score . Card #4's link is wrong : the sheet says FurMark 5,103 but the linked result belongs to a PowerColor RX 9070 XT scoring 15,590 . That is an erroneous citation, not proof that card #4 is an AMD GPU . All 36 matched GTX 1070 public submissions share the PCI device ID 10DE:1B81 and reported subsystem 7377:0000 . PCI-SIG assigns vendor 7377 to Shenzhen Colorful Yugong Technology and Development Co., Ltd , rather than Gigabyte [1]. This conflicts with an earlier photographed-label identification as Gigabyte GTX 1070 WINDFORCE OC 8G Rev. 2.0 [2]. It does not automatically mean counterfeit or modified cards: a firmware-reported PCI ID, a physical shroud/label and one earlier identification must be reconciled, not conflated. Exact board branding is not yet independently verified across the batch . These public FurMark runs show 50–66°C peak reported GPU temperature and 99% peak GPU utilisation in many results. Encouraging for a 60-second load, not proof of VRAM health, acoustics or sustained reliability . The three testing PCs have different CPUs and NVIDIA drivers , making a simple 'highest score = best physical GPU' ranking unreliable.

title: My GTX 1070 batch: deep research
h: 1. The silicon and history
t: 1. The silicon and history NVIDIA launched the GeForce GTX 1070 on 10 June 2016 , built on its Pascal architecture and the GP104 chip [3]. It originally offered previous-generation flagship-class raster performance for US 379 p a r t n e r / U S 449 Founders Edition at launch. This is historic US pricing, not its value in Australia today. GPU feature Reference GTX 1070 GPU family NVIDIA Pascal GP104, desktop CUDA cores 1,920 TMUs / ROPs 120 / 64 Fabrication 16 nm Video memory 8 GB GDDR5 Bus / bandwidth 256 bit / approx. 256 GB/s Reference clocks approx. 1,506 MHz base / 1,683 MHz boost Reference board power 150 W ; actual partner/VBIOS power limit may vary Expansion bus PCIe 3.0 x16 Supplemental power commonly one 8-pin on reference-type boards; check each physical card Gaming strengths in 2026 older/lighter games at 1080p, retro gaming and compatible compute tasks Gaming limitations no dedicated RTX ray-tracing cores, Tensor cores or hardware DLSS NVIDIA's launch account and contemporary GPU specification lists support these characteristics [3][4][5]. The GPU was a strong 1440p option in 2016. Ten years later, it remains useful for lower-cost machines, but modern high-fidelity games and current AI tooling can exceed its capabilities. 8 GB VRAM does not turn a Pascal GPU into a modern RTX GPU. The board-model question is more complicated An earlier physical photograph was identified as Gigabyte GV-N1070WF2OC-8GD Rev. 2.0 . If that identification is accurate for a specific card, Gigabyte's official specs [2] list a WINDFORCE 2X dual-fan cooler, 6+2 power phases , 1771/1582 MHz OC-mode boost/base , 1746/1556 MHz gaming boost/base , 280 x 131 x 37 mm , one 8-pin PCIe and outputs 3 DisplayPort, HDMI, DVI-D . These are model-specific, not automatically applicable to all 36 matched public results . The result pages instead report 7377:0000 . The PCI-SIG member directory identifies 0x7377 as Colorful [1], and independent Linux hardware records resolve the same GPU + subsystem to Colorful [6]. Colorful sold several GTX 1070 designs with differing cooling and power connectors [7]. title: My GTX 1070 batch: deep research
h: 4. What do the results prove about health?
t: 4. What do the results prove about health? Proven for many tested examples: GPU-Z initialisation and the ability to complete a short high-load rendering test; for 35 cards, three scores appear in the sheet. Not yet proven across the batch: memory correctness, all outputs functioning, stable operation after sustained warm-up, acceptable fan-bearing sound, correct original firmware, no power/connector damage, or genuine provenance. A useful minimal, non-redundant grading workflow: Identify the exact physical board. Give each unit a numbered sticker, record model/revision/serial privately and GPU-Z details. An identical PCI model does not uniquely distinguish two physical cards. Inspect while powered off. Fans spin without rubbing, no missing blades/loose screws, burnt connectors or damaged PCB. On any mechanical noise (#36), stop before further load . Repeatable render checks. Keep consistent FurMark P1080 GL, same settings and a recorded test rig/driver. Use Superposition and/or standard Steel Nomad as different rendering workloads, not endless duplicates of FurMark. Test memory/errors. Add a VRAM-error test such as OCCT VRAM, and log duration and actual error count . The Sheet only has 'No errors' notes for #18–20; that must not be extrapolated to other rows. Inspect function and acoustics. Test HDMI/DisplayPort outputs and fan response at idle and at moderate load. For cards intended to be resold, a calm, repeatable functional check matters more than a peak score. Grade transparently. 'Fully tested', 'runs but incomplete', 'needs diagnosis' and 'faulty (verified)' are distinct statuses. Missing tests are unknown , not passes or fails. Provide the actual test date and links when advertising. NVIDIA cautions FurMark can draw more power than normal games and that disabling over-temperature/over-current protections can damage cards [12]. Never bypass those protections , and stop on artefacts, abnormal sounds, unexpected shutdowns or unsafe heat. A 60-second peak temperature of 50°C does not establish a better cooler than another board peaking at 66°C: room conditions, fan speeds, clocks and actual GPU watts matter.

title: My GTX 1070 batch: deep research
h: 5. Drivers, Windows, AI and realistic 2026 use
t: 5. Drivers, Windows, AI and realistic 2026 use Driver lifecycle: NVIDIA's official Pascal/Maxwell/Volta policy says Game Ready feature/performance updates ended in October 2025 , with critical security driver updates continuing through October 2028 [13]. The presence of a newer-numbered driver does not imply new gaming capabilities. Windows 10: All validated public score pages say Windows 10 build 19045 . Microsoft ended ordinary Windows 10 support on 14 October 2025 , although Extended Security Updates are available for eligible enrolled machines [14]. The benchmark records cannot establish whether a tester is enrolled. Avoid treating an unpatched online test box as a safe everyday workstation. Compute/AI: NVIDIA lists the GTX 1070 at CUDA compute capability 6.1 [15]. CUDA Toolkit 13 removed offline compilation support for architectures older than capability 7.5; older CUDA toolkit paths may be needed for legacy GPU projects [16]. No Tensor cores, no RTX/DLSS and no compelling performance for modern large generative models. These are still good low-cost GPUs for legacy graphics research, older games and compatible image/video workflows, subject to application support. Hardware fit: Full-size PCIe slot and the exact board's video outputs, external power connector(s), dimensions, PSU, cooling and BIOS compatibility must be checked before recommending a card for a particular desktop. A laptop cannot simply accept a desktop PCIe GTX 1070 internally . The actual current GPU and whether the machine is still owned must be established before claiming an upgrade.

h: 7. What is still genuinely unknown?
t: 7. What is still genuinely unknown? Physical count and ownership history: 100 sheet slots do not mean 100 GPUs ; earlier conversation referred to a batch of 92 , not fully reconciled against labels. The board manufacturer, actual submodel, serial, original VBIOS and memory chip vendor per card . Colorful PCI subsystem vs earlier Gigabyte label is an open evidence conflict. Whether card #4's actual FurMark submission can be recovered. Do not silently replace the wrong AMD result with a guessed link. Why card #36's fan is loud, and whether it is repairable. A same-PC, same-driver, same-preset fair ranking of the batch. Universal VRAM, output and fan tests (not present yet). Whether any card was previously used for mining. Do not assume mining history merely from quantity. Actual Australian sold prices and net resale proceeds. Superposition's exact test preset/API and Steel Nomad edition for every entry. Research conclusion: the known GTX 1070 results are broadly consistent and their short-run temperatures look reasonable. The physical manufacturer conflict , wrong #4 link , noisy #36 , two incomplete card records and VRAM/port/fan certification gaps are more important to resolve than chasing an additional few points in FurMark.

title: How this site is built: web best practices applied
h: The short version
t: The short version Four bodies of evidence agree on what matters: pages that load fast and stay still (Core Web Vitals), that everyone can use (WCAG 2.2), that say clearly what they are to people and search engines (Google's SEO guide), and that respect how people actually read (scanning, not reading) [1][2][3][4][5][6]. Measured with Lighthouse on the published site, the home page started at 81 for performance and 85 for accessibility, and the reading pages at 98 and 84. After the changes below, both kinds of page score 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO, and 99 or 100 for performance in lab runs, with the home page's first paint nearly twice as fast (see "Measured results").

title: How this site is built: web best practices applied
h: What the research says
t: What the research says Speed and stability: Core Web Vitals. Google's three user-experience metrics have fixed "good" thresholds, judged on at least 75% of page visits: Largest Contentful Paint 2.5 seconds or less, Interaction to Next Paint 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift 0.1 or less [1][2][3][4]. The specific advice that matters for a static site like this one: Always give images and videos width and height (or CSS aspect-ratio ) so the browser reserves space before they load; web fonts that swap can also shift layout, so fallback fonts should match the web font's metrics [3][7]. Fonts: self-host WOFF2 files, preload only the critical face, use font-display , and be cautious with preload because it competes with other critical requests [7]. Images: choose a modern format. WebP and AVIF compress better than JPEG and PNG and are widely supported [8]. Interaction responsiveness comes down to the main thread: long tasks delay input, so break up or remove heavy work [4]. Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 and what actually fails. WebAIM's 2025 analysis of one million home pages found WCAG failures on 94.8% of them. The commonest was low-contrast text on 79.1% of pages , followed by missing image descriptions, missing form labels, empty links and buttons, and a missing document language [5]. WCAG 2.2 added criteria that matter for an interactive page like this one: target size of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (2.5.8) , a non-dragging alternative for any drag interaction (2.5.7) , and focus must not be hidden behind sticky bars (2.4.11) [9]. Search and sharing: Google's SEO starter guide. Unique, accurate titles and page-specific descriptions; descriptive link text; descriptive alt text; a canonical URL where duplicates are possible; images placed near relevant text; and a sitemap to help crawlers find pages [6]. Social preview cards (Open Graph) are not Google guidance but are the de facto standard for how a link looks when shared. Reading: people scan. Nielsen Norman Group's research found that 79% of test users always scanned a new page and only 16% read word by word [10]. The practical consequences are meaningful headings, short paragraphs, lists, and a table of contents.

title: How this site is built: web best practices applied
h: What was changed, and why
t: What was changed, and why Finding Change on this site Fonts should be self-hosted, and a third-party font stylesheet is an extra request that blocks first render [7] The three fonts are now self-hosted Latin subsets (Space Grotesk 22 KB, JetBrains Mono 31 KB, Newsreader 58 KB, pinned to one optical size), with the font CSS inlined and the main font preloaded. Swapping fonts can shift layout [3][7] Added size-matched fallback fonts , so the swap barely moves text. Images need dimensions and modern formats [3][8] The seven photographs are WebP (about 40% smaller, 1.1 MB to 0.6 MB), with width , height and decoding="async" ; video thumbnails got dimensions too. Long tasks hurt responsiveness [4] The hero animation draws 1,500 strands instead of 3,600 , allocates nothing per frame, starts after the first paint, caps its frame rate, adapts its density to the device , and pauses off-screen or in a hidden tab. Decorative canvas art and the 70-question explorer now load only when you scroll near them. Low contrast is the top failure [5] The faint-text colour was darkened or lightened to pass 4.5:1 in both themes. Colour alone must not signal a link (WCAG 1.4.1) [9] Links inside running text are underlined. Targets must be 24 px (2.5.8) [9] Citation markers, chart rows, buttons and chips now meet the minimum. Dragging needs an alternative (2.5.7) [9] The hero torus rotates with the arrow keys as well as by dragging. Accessible names must contain visible text; heading levels must not skip [5][9] Chart rows start their accessible name with the visible label; footer and calculator headings were fixed; the logo link has a name. Descriptive titles, canonical URLs, sitemap [6] Canonical URLs, sitemap.xml , robots.txt , per-page descriptions, breadcrumbs, and JSON-LD (WebSite on the home page; Article and BreadcrumbList on each reading page). Shared links need a preview Open Graph and Twitter card metadata with a 1200 by 630 preview image. A missing favicon logged a 404 on every page Added an SVG favicon , touch icon and a web app manifest with theme colour. People scan [10] Reading pages already had a table of contents, reading time and hover-to-preview citations; they now also have breadcrumbs, an "updated" date and a print stylesheet that expands links into the page. Broken links should lead somewhere A real 404 page with routes back into the site.

h: Measured results
t: Measured results Lighthouse (mobile profile, simulated slow connection) on the published site, before the changes and after them: Page Performance Accessibility Best practices SEO First paint Blocking time Layout shift Home, before 81 85 96 100 1.9 s 690 ms 0 Home, after 99 to 100 100 100 100 1.0 s 10 to 120 ms 0.04 A reading page, before 98 84 96 100 1.8 s 0 ms 0 A reading page, after 100 100 100 100 0.9 s 0 to 30 ms 0 to 0.004 Lab scores vary from run to run, especially for the home page, which animates. The home page's layout shift rose from 0 to 0.04 because more content now renders after the data loads; that is still inside the 0.1 "good" threshold [3]. Field data from real visitors is not available for a site this new, and this site collects no analytics.

title: How this site is built: web best practices applied
h: Considered and left out
t: Considered and left out content-visibility: auto on page sections. It skips rendering of off-screen sections, but it also made the browser report empty text for controls that had not been scrolled into view, which broke the repository's own browser tests and could confuse other tools. Total Blocking Time was already near zero without it. A service worker for offline use. Cached copies can serve stale pages while the site is still changing daily; the gain does not outweigh the confusion. Analytics. Not needed, and it would add a third party and a consent question. A strict Content Security Policy. The pages use inline styles and scripts, so a meta-tag policy would have to allow them and protect little. Dark-mode-only. The site defaults to dark, with a light theme behind the toggle; both pass contrast checks.
